Figures 9 and 10 plot the resulting error histories for \(u\) and \(v\). In all four problems, the errors start at zero and grow monotonically without numerical oscillations, reaching their maxima at \(T=0.01\). For the one-soliton, Gaussian, and sinusoidal tests, the growth is nearly linear in \(t\), with the ratio \(E_u(t)/t\) varying by less than \(10\%\) over the interval; on the logarithmic vertical scale, this steady accumulation appears as a smooth concave curve. The two-soliton case follows the same near-linear trend up to about \(t=0.009\) and then steepens, with \(E_u(t)/t\) increasing by \(36\%\) over the final tenth of the run. This late-stage steepening corresponds to the time window in which the two soliton branches meet and form sharper gradients on the scale of the grid.

Comparing the three curves within each panel, we see that RK4 and Crank–Nicolson lie on top of each other throughout the entire evolution, whereas the forward Euler curve is shifted vertically by a factor that remains nearly constant in time. For \(u\) (Figure 9), the Euler curve lies below RK4 by factors near \(0.99\), \(0.18\), and \(0.62\) in the one-soliton, Gaussian, and sinusoidal tests, and drifts from \(0.97\) to \(0.79\) during the two-soliton interaction. For \(v\) (Figure 10), the Euler curve follows the same shape but is displaced above RK4 — by factors of \(1.04\) and \(1.08\) in the two soliton tests and \(8.2\) and \(9.0\) in the Gaussian and sinusoidal tests.
